author: bdnews24.com
title: Twin votes: Is EC ready for referendum with general election?
text:
Published : 09 Oct 2025, 02:17 AM
As the Election Commission (EC) advances preparations for the parliamentary election, debate has returned to the national conversation over a referendum to implement the July Charter.
The commission says it has no separate plan for a referendum outside the parliamentary polls. If the government decides, however, the EC will work to implement it.
Election Commissioner Abdur Rahmanel Masud said holding a referendum on the same day as the parliamentary election would save "hundreds upon millions of taka".
The National Consensus Commission also says there is broad agreement on holding a referendum to implement the July Charter. Some parties propose holding the referendum and the parliamentary election on the same day, while others propose holding the referendum a month before the general election.
For a parliamentary electorate of over 126.3 million voters, there will be more than 40,000 polling centres and over 250,000 polling booths. For the first time, arrangements are being made to take the votes of expatriate Bangladeshis through IT-supported postal ballots.
The parliamentary election, costing around Tk 25 billion, will engage more than one million personnel.
Under the EC led by AMM Nasir Uddin, the parliamentary election is slated for the first half of February, before Ramadan, with the schedule to be announced in December.
The immediate question is this: if a referendum is to be held pursuant to the National Consensus Commission’s process, how capable is the EC of organising it within four months? The country is also revisiting Bangladesh’s past experience with referendums.
WHAT IS THE EC THINKING?
Bangladesh has held three referendums: in 1977 to test confidence in the president, in 1985 to legitimise military rule, and in 1991 on constitutional change.
Asked how prepared the EC is to hold a referendum before or alongside the national polls, Election Commissioner Abdur Rahmanel Masud told bdnews24.com: “From what we see in the papers, at this moment it depends on political consensus. This decision is a matter of state, a government matter. If the government decides to hold a referendum, we will hold it.”
He believes significant savings would be made if it is held together with the parliamentary election.
“It is difficult to conduct such an expensive exercise on two separate days,” he said, “If the government decides, that is not our call. Combining the two polls would save a lot of money.”
If the election is in February, holding both on the same day is feasible, Masud added.
“A parliamentary election and a referendum can be held together. Some additional polling centres and booths may be needed. It is not impossible; indeed, better together.”
Drawing on his judicial and legal experience, the commissioner said he sees no legal impediment.
“The people are the source of all power. A question is being placed before them via the July Charter: are you in favour or against? If there is a people’s verdict, that is the greatest strength. If minor legal adjustments are needed, the government will make them (if required). If the government or the Consensus Commission takes such a decision, we will see how to implement it within the legal framework.”
Masud added that holding a referendum within the national election timetable would not affect the February schedule.
“Indeed, combining them would save hundreds of millions of taka. Separate days mean extra cost, strain, recruitment, and innumerable arrangements.
"If done together, it is better for the country. Centres, voters, returning officers, polling staff -- all remain the same; there are simply two ballot papers: one for the parliamentary election and one for a standard referendum.”
THE THREE PAST REFERENDUMS
A referendum is a process for taking the people’s direct opinion on major questions of state, presenting a significant issue for final acceptance or rejection.
Since independence, referendums have been held three times: 1977, 1985, and 1991.
May 30, 1977: The first referendum sought public opinion on the then president Ziaur Rahman and the policies and programmes he pursued.
Result: 98.8% “Yes”, 1.12% “No.”
Mar 21, 1985: The second asked voters to express confidence in the policies and programmes of the then president Hussain Muhammad Ershad and to agree that he remain president until elections under the suspended constitution -- in essence, to legitimise military rule.
Result: 94.11% “Yes”, 5.50% “No”
Sept 15, 1991: Under Article 142(1A), the third referendum asked whether the president should assent to the 12th Amendment Bill, 1991, effectively posing the choice of future system of government.
Result: 84% “Yes”, 15.62% “No.”
LAW CHANGES NEEDED FOR REFERENDUM
Nizam Uddin Ahmed, a parliamentary affairs researcher and former professor at the University of Chittagong, says the easiest route now is to hold the referendum alongside the national ballot.
“You are not amending the Constitution to do that. You are placing proposed constitutional amendments before the people. If the people accept them, they will be implemented by the next Parliament. The referendum would be a popular mandate.
“This does not amend the Constitution by itself, nor does it breach the president’s powers. The president cannot amend the Constitution by ordinance. Therefore, there is no barrier to a referendum.”
Nizam notes that referendum provisions were repealed in 2011, but this year the High Court delivered a judgment to bring back the referendum concept.
“If the government wishes to test public opinion, it may hold a referendum. If people consent, the new parliament can introduce the amendments through the constitutional process.”
“There is provision for referendums on four specific articles. Legally, there is no obstacle. The High Court’s verdict in the caretaker government case speaks of restoring the referendum. To conduct one, the RPO (Representation of the People Order) would need amending, and the EC must be instructed to hold the referendum.”
Nizam believes two referendums may be needed. Ordinarily, a referendum poses one yes or no question.
First, a referendum would seek public consent to proceed with reforms based on the July Charter.
Later, as constitutional amendments become necessary to implement the Charter’s 84 reforms, a second referendum would be required.
“If you reduce the powers of the president and prime minister, or decentralise aspects of the Supreme Court/High Court, some referendums will be unavoidable,” Nizam said.
Citing global practice, he adds that many countries pair referendums with general elections.
“It’s a good initiative to exit the crisis. The 1991 Referendum Act and Rules exist; amend them and it can be done. Holding both together also reduces confusion. People are used to casting three ballots in Union Parishad election, here there would be two. I see no barrier to a referendum.”
WHAT DOES THE MOST RECENT EXPERIENCE SAY?
Mihir Sarwar Morshed, a former EC official involved in organising the 1991 referendum, recalls: “That referendum concerned the 12th Amendment -- a yes or no vote on returning from a presidential to a parliamentary system. Deputy commissioners acted as returning officers.”
“Public interest in referendums is usually quite low. Newspapers of the time show low turnout, although the results can be emphatic. Referendums rarely produce tribunal cases or complications; the declared result generally stands.”
He notes that the 1991 referendum was held after the general election and conducted under the Referendum Act and Rules.
Holding both together now would be better, he says. Polling stations would require as many ballot boxes for the referendum as for the parliamentary polls.
“There are no candidates, no voter slips, and voters are not formally invited with the same ceremony, so lower interest and attendance. If political parties help this time, turnout may improve.”
OPERATIONAL READINESS, VOTER EDUCATION
According to Abdul Alim, a member of the Electoral Reform Commission, “A referendum and a parliamentary election are two different exercises and require separate ballot papers and separate ballot boxes. The EC would need to prepare two kinds of ballot papers and segregate ballot boxes.”
“People last voted in a referendum in 1991; the instrument has been largely forgotten. There is a public knowledge gap. We will need wide outreach and civic education on what a referendum is and why it matters; otherwise voters will lack the information needed to exercise their choice.”
He lists the practical challenges: printing ballot papers, procuring transparent ballot boxes, training polling officials, and engaging voters in the process. If a decision is taken quickly, he believes the EC would not be unduly challenged.
Given voters’ experience of using three ballot papers in local government elections, he expects no great difficulty in explaining a two-ballot process if the parliamentary election and referendum are held together.
“Everyone now broadly agrees on holding a referendum; the timing is where opinions differ. Consensus is crucial -- if the parties agree, no major challenge remains.”
BEFORE AND AFTER: LEGAL TRAJECTORY OF REFERENDUMS
The Electoral Reform Commission has recommended tabling and passing a referendum provision in the next parliament.
Bangladesh’s original 1972 Constitution had no referendum clause. In 1979, Zia introduced the Fifth Amendment, which added Article 142(1A) on constitutional amendments and referendums.
It provided that, notwithstanding Article 142(1), if a bill amending the Preamble or Articles 8, 48, 56, 58, 80 or 90A, or provisions of Article 142 itself, was passed and presented to the president for assent, the [resident would, within seven days, refer the question of assent to a referendum.
The Fifth Amendment also added Articles 142(1B), (1C) and (1D) on referendums.
In 1991, to restore parliamentary democracy through the 12th Amendment, the scope of Article 142(1A) was narrowed by removing the referendum requirement for amendments to Articles 58, 80 and 90A -- leaving mandatory referendums for amendments to the Preamble, and Articles 8, 48 or 56.
Under the 15th Amendment, passed on Jun 30, 2011 during the Awami League government, Article 142 was replaced and the referendum provision abolished.
However, on Dec 17, 2024, in litigation concerning the 15th Amendment, the court struck down Article 142 as amended and spoke of reviving the referendum provision.
There remains a question whether the provision was automatically reinstated. Under Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, to revive a repealed law, parliament must pass legislation.
The Electoral Reform Commission therefore argues that a parliamentary enactment is required to formally restore the referendum clause.
